lesson_title: One Little Number: Why H2O Is Water and H2O2 Is Bleach
hook_text: Add one oxygen atom to water and you get something you must never drink.
clip_script: A chemical formula is a recipe card, and the recipe never changes. H2O: two hydrogens, one oxygen. Every glass of pure water on Earth, from the Vaal to the sea, is exactly two to one. The rule for reading it: the little number belongs to the letter right before it, and no number means one. So CO2 is one carbon, two oxygens, not two carbons. Brackets are packets: Ca(OH)2 is one calcium and two packets of OH, so two oxygens and two hydrogens. Now the danger. Change one little number and you change the substance. H2O is water. H2O2 is hydrogen peroxide, which bleaches hair and kills germs. Do not drink it. CO2 is the gas you breathe out. CO, one oxygen fewer, is carbon monoxide, no colour, no smell, and it kills people who run braziers in closed rooms every winter. One little number. Completely different stuff. That is why chemists never touch the subscripts.
visual_style: Recipe cards flip to show H2O and CO2 built from coloured balls; a bracket opens like a packet; a single extra red ball snaps onto water and the label changes to a warning sign; a brazier in a closed room fades to a CO warning.
pacing: Fast recipe beats, a clear rule beat, a dramatic pause before each one-number change, a firm closing line.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and count every atom in glucose.
